screens.title: Direct‑Mapped, Set‑Associative, and Fully‑Associative Caches
screens.narratorSegment: Today we study three cache mapping strategies that determine where memory blocks live inside a cache. You will learn the defining property of each mapping, the step-by-step access procedure they use, and why associativity changes hit rate, access time, area, and power. We’ll ground the ideas with a 32 KB example so you can see actual numbers for lines, sets, and tag overhead. Understanding these mappings matters because the cache is the first hardware your processor relies on for speed: a wrong design increases misses, slows execution, and burns more power. For example, a direct‑mapped L1 is simple and very fast, but two hot blocks can repeatedly evict each other and cause conflict misses. A set‑associative design reduces those conflicts by giving blocks multiple candidate lines, and a fully‑associative cache eliminates conflict misses entirely at the cost of parallel tag comparisons and larger area. By the end you’ll be able to calculate index and tag bits, compare access-time tradeoffs, and make evidence-based choices for L1 and L2 design. Ask yourself as we go: for a given working set, when is extra associativity worth the hardware cost?

Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Overview

Cache mapping strategies

Direct‑mapped, set‑associative, and fully‑associative choices and why they matter for L1 and L2 caches.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Quick formulas
CacheLine = (BlockAddress) mod (NumberOfCacheLines)
Set = (BlockAddress) mod (NumberOfSets)

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will build measurable skills that let you design and evaluate caches. First, you will learn to design and analyze a direct‑mapped cache: extracting index and offset bits, storing tags and valid/dirty bits, and detecting hits precisely. That skill matters because correct indexing and tag width are foundational to cache correctness and accurate area/power estimates. Second, you will implement set‑associative caches and understand replacement policies like least‑recently‑used and random replacement; you will see how the replacement policy affects effective hit rate and implementation complexity. Third, you will develop intuition for how associativity changes hit rate, access time, and power — including why returns diminish as associativity grows. Finally, you will calculate area and tag overhead for real cache designs, using formulas that combine data bits and tag bits. Each objective pairs a definition with a concrete calculation or small example so you can reason quantitatively. By the end you will be able to justify a cache organization for an L1 or L2 based on measured tradeoffs and simple area math.

screens.title: Direct‑Mapped Cache Mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: A direct‑mapped cache places each memory block into exactly one cache line determined by the block address modulo the number of cache lines. Practically, that means the address is partitioned into offset bits, index bits, and tag bits. The offset selects a byte within a line, the index selects a specific cache line, and the tag distinguishes different blocks that map to the same line. The access procedure is deterministic: extract the index, read the stored tag and valid bit for that line, compare tags, and if they match and valid is set, it's a hit; otherwise fetch from the next level. A concrete example helps: with a 32 KB cache and 64‑byte lines we have 512 lines; offset is 6 bits, index is 9 bits, and the remaining address bits form the tag. A common misconception is that direct mapping is always too poor for performance — in fact, for many streaming or tightly localized workloads it performs well due to its low latency and minimal hardware. The core tradeoff to watch for is conflict misses: two frequently used blocks that share the same index will repeatedly evict each other. A key takeaway is that direct mapping is the fastest and smallest design but you must consider access patterns to avoid pathological conflicts. How might your program’s stride create repeated conflicts?

keyIdea.title: Deterministic mapping
keyIdea.text: Direct mapping is simple and fast: index selects a single line, tag and valid bits detect hits.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Direct‑Mapped Cache
Definition & access steps
  1. Extract offset and index from address.
  2. Read the tag and valid bit for the indexed line.
  3. Compare tag; if match and valid, it's a hit; otherwise miss.
  4. On miss, fetch block and replace the line (update valid/dirty accordingly).
Concrete example
32 KB cache, 64‑byte line → 512 lines
Offset = 6 bits, Index = 9 bits, Tag = 32 - 6 - 9 = 17 bits.
Common misconception

Simplicity equals poor performance. In many workloads the simplicity gives lower latency and fewer dynamic power costs, making direct mapping competitive when access patterns are friendly.

Visual: line layout
Tag array
512 tags of 17 bits + valid + dirty
Data array
512 × 64 bytes = 32 KB
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Direct mapping is the fastest and simplest mapping. Watch for conflict misses when multiple hot blocks map to the same index.

screens.title: Set‑Associative Caches and Access Procedure
screens.narratorSegment: A set‑associative cache generalizes direct mapping by grouping lines into sets and allowing a block to occupy any line within its set. The set index is computed as block address modulo the number of sets and the set contains N ways. Access proceeds by extracting the set index, then reading and comparing N tags and valid bits in parallel. If one matches and is valid, the access is a hit and the offset selects bytes within that way. If none match, a replacement is required: the cache chooses a victim line within the set according to the replacement policy — common policies are least‑recently‑used (LRU) and random replacement. A concrete example: a 4‑way, 32 KB cache with 64‑byte lines has 128 sets; each set stores four tags and four valid bits, and four comparators are used concurrently. A common misconception is that associativity alone removes all misses; it only eliminates conflict misses but not capacity or compulsory misses. The practical implication is that set associativity reduces conflicts with modest hardware cost when N is small, but returns diminish as N grows. Consider: if two hot blocks map to the same set, a 2‑way design may fix it, but increasing to 16‑way may add complexity without meaningful hit-rate gain. What replacement policy would you choose for a small embedded L1 cache and why?

keyIdea.title: Parallel tag checks
keyIdea.text: Set‑associative caches read multiple tags in parallel and use a replacement policy when a miss occurs in the set.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Set‑Associative Cache
Access procedure (N‑way)
  1. Compute set index from block address.
  2. Read N tags and valid bits for that set in parallel.
  3. Compare all tags simultaneously; if a valid match exists, it's a hit.
  4. On miss, choose a victim line via replacement policy and write back if dirty.
Replacement policies
LRU: evict least recently used — good hit-rate, higher tracking cost
Random: low hardware cost, sometimes competitive in practice
Concrete example

4‑way, 32 KB, 64‑byte: sets = 128, each access compares 4 tags in parallel. This reduces conflicts compared with direct mapping while adding comparators and multiplexers.

Visual: set layout
One set (4 ways)
Way 0: tag, valid, dirty • Way 1: tag, valid, dirty • Way 2 • Way 3
Hardware cost
N comparators and a multiplexer per set increase area and power roughly with N.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Set associativity reduces conflict misses by offering multiple candidate lines but requires parallel comparators and replacement logic.

screens.title: Fully‑Associative Cache Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: A fully‑associative cache allows any memory block to occupy any cache line. There is no index; the cache compares the address tag against all stored tags simultaneously. This eliminates conflict misses because a block never has a fixed destination, but achieving this behavior requires comparators and search logic across the entire cache, which increases area and power. Fully associativity is therefore rare for large data caches but valuable for small structures where conflict should be avoided — for example, TLBs or small victim caches. A concrete example: a small 64‑line fully‑associative structure will compare one tag against 64 stored tags in parallel; hardware designers often use CAM‑style techniques or optimized comparators. A common misconception is that fully‑associative caches always give the best performance; they do minimize conflicts but their slower access time and power can make overall system performance worse if the comparator delay increases critical path latency. The main design question is cost versus conflict reduction. Reflect: for which small hardware structure could you afford full associativity and why? Fully‑Associative Cache Behavior means fully-associative caches remove conflict misses but cost significant comparators, area, and power; used where small size or special semantics justify it.. In practical terms, any line can hold any block; tags compared against all lines. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: No index, all tags compared
keyIdea.text: Fully-associative caches remove conflict misses but cost significant comparators, area, and power; used where small size or special semantics justify it.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Fully‑Associative Cache
How it works

There is no index field; the tag field of the address is compared against every tag entry. If any valid entry matches, it’s a hit. On miss, any line may be replaced.

When to use
Small structures like TLBs, victim caches, or specialized buffers where conflict misses are particularly harmful.
Misconception

Higher hit rate always wins. In reality, larger comparator arrays increase access time and power and may harm overall performance for latency‑sensitive caches.

Concrete snapshot
  • Example: 64‑line fully‑associative cache compares 64 tags in parallel.
  • Cost: comparators scale with number of lines; multiplexing data out requires larger routing.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Fully‑associative removes conflicts but at high hardware cost. Use it when small size or special semantics make conflict tolerance worth the expense.

screens.title: Hit Rate, Access Time, Area, and Power
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing mapping types requires balancing four core metrics: hit rate, access time, area, and power. Direct‑mapped caches have the smallest area and lowest power because they need one comparator per access and minimal multiplexing, so access time is fastest. However, they suffer more conflict misses, giving the lowest hit rate in adversarial mapping scenarios. Set‑associative caches improve hit rate by offering multiple candidate lines per set; they need N comparators and multiplexers which increase area, power, and nominal access time in proportion to N. Fully‑associative caches give the highest hit rate because they eliminate conflict misses, but they are the most expensive in area and power and typically have the longest access latency because of the large number of parallel comparators. A useful rule of thumb drawn from practical systems: 2‑ to 8‑way associativity is common in L1 caches where low latency is critical; L2 caches may use higher associativity since their latency budget is larger. One misconception is that associativity always yields consistent benefit — in practice returns diminish as you increase associativity because remaining misses become capacity or compulsory misses. As a design question, ask whether the hit-rate gain from increasing associativity justifies the extra comparator and multiplexer cost for your target workload.

keyIdea.title: Four-way tradeoff
keyIdea.text: Higher associativity increases hit rate but also increases comparator count, access time, area, and power; diminishing returns apply.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Tradeoff Comparison
Comparison table (qualitative)
Direct-Mapped
  • Hit rate: lowest
  • Access time: fastest
  • Area/power: smallest
Set-Associative
  • Hit rate: medium
  • Access time: medium
  • Area/power: medium
Fully-Associative
  • Hit rate: highest
  • Access time: slowest
  • Area/power: largest
Design guidance

For latency-critical L1 caches use lower associativity (2–8 ways). For L2, higher associativity is acceptable because the latency budget is larger and conflict reduction can improve performance.

Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Pick associativity to trade off hit rate against comparator and multiplexer cost; measure diminishing returns as N grows.

screens.title: Index, Offset, and Tag Bit Calculations
screens.narratorSegment: Computing offset, index, and tag bits is a fundamental step when designing caches. Start with line size L: offset bits equal log2(L) because the offset selects the byte within a line. Number of lines equals S divided by L. For associativity A, the number of sets equals S divided by (L × A), so index bits equal log2(number of sets). The remaining bits of the address width become the tag. Concretely, for a 32 KB cache with 64‑byte lines and 4‑way associativity: offset = log2(64) = 6, sets = 32768 / (64 × 4) = 128, index = log2(128) = 7, so tag = 32 - 6 - 7 = 19. A common error is forgetting to divide by associativity when computing sets — this produces an incorrect index width and wrong mapping. Below is a small code-like checklist you can use when doing the math yourself. Practice this computation on the three designs in the hands‑on exercise to see how index bits change between direct, 4‑way and 8‑way. Remember to include valid and dirty bits when calculating tag storage overhead.

keyIdea.title: Bit partitioning
keyIdea.text: Offset = log2(L), Index = log2(S / (L×A)), Tag = AddressWidth − offset − index.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Bit Calculations
Step-by-step checklist
// Given: S (cache bytes), L (line bytes), A (associativity), W (address bits)
offset = log2(L)
lines = S / L
sets = S / (L * A)
index = log2(sets)
tag = W - offset - index
// Include valid + dirty bits per line when computing tag storage
Common pitfall: using lines instead of sets for index when A > 1. Always divide by associativity to get the set count.
Worked example
  • 32 KB, 64‑byte, 4‑way: offset=6, sets=128, index=7, tag=19.
  • Direct (1‑way): sets=512, index=9, tag=17.
  • 8‑way: sets=64, index=6, tag=20.
Key Takeaway

Index width decreases as associativity increases because each set holds more lines; tag width increases accordingly for fixed address width.

screens.title: Area Calculation and Tag Overhead
screens.narratorSegment: Calculating cache area starts with the data array and the tag array. For a cache of size S, the data array stores S × 8 bits. The tag array stores a tag per line: tag bits plus one valid bit and one dirty bit for write‑back caches. The number of lines equals S divided by L, so tag storage in bits equals (S / L) × (T + 1 + 1), where T is the tag size in bits. The total area is data area plus tag area plus modest overhead for decoders, comparators, and multiplexers. A concrete example given in the chapter: with 64‑byte lines and 32‑bit addresses, the tag is about 20 bits plus 2 status bits, so the tag overhead per line is 22 bits, which is 22 / 512 = 4.3% for 64‑byte lines. For 32‑byte lines the overhead doubles to 8.6% because the denominator halves. A common mistake is omitting the valid and dirty bits when computing tag area — these add directly to the tag storage and can be nontrivial for small line sizes. When designing, inspect how line size affects overhead: larger lines reduce tag overhead but can increase wasted data transfer on partial-line utilization. What line size would you pick for a workload with frequent small random accesses?

keyIdea.title: Data + tag math
keyIdea.text: Total area ≈ data bits (S×8) + tag bits ((S/L)×(T+valid+dirty)) plus overhead for comparators and control.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Area & Tag Overhead
Formulas
Data array bits = S × 8
Lines = S / L
Tag array bits = Lines × (T + 1 valid + 1 dirty)
Total ≈ Data array + Tag array + overhead
Tag overhead percentage = Tag array bits / Data array bits.
Worked numbers
  • 64‑byte lines, 32‑bit address → T ≈ 20 bits; T+2 = 22 bits → overhead = 22 / 512 = 4.3%.
  • 32‑byte lines → overhead ≈ 8.6% because fewer data bits per line.
Key Takeaway

Tag overhead is sensitive to line size. Small lines raise tag overhead; large lines reduce overhead but may increase wasted data movement.

screens.title: Design Exercise: 32 KB Cache Variants
screens.narratorSegment: This practical exercise walks you through comparing three 32 KB cache designs: direct‑mapped, 4‑way, and 8‑way, all with 64‑byte lines. screens.title: Replacement Policies and Practical Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Replacement policy choice impacts effective hit rate and hardware cost. LRU approximates the least recently used line and often gives the best hit rate for workloads with temporal locality, but implementing exact LRU becomes expensive as associativity grows because it requires tracking order among N ways. Random replacement is cheap — it avoids the complexity of counters or LRU stacks — and surprisingly effective for some workloads, especially when associativity is already moderate. A practical pitfall is assuming LRU always wins; in some traces random or pseudo‑LRU delivers similar results for a fraction of the hardware cost. Another frequent mistake is ignoring write behavior: for write‑back caches you must track dirty bits and write back evicted dirty lines, which affects bandwidth and energy. A concrete example: in a 4‑way cache, exact LRU tracking needs bits or small counters per line and an update on each hit, which adds critical path activity. When designing an L1, weigh the benefit of a slightly higher hit rate against increased access time and power from complex replacement logic. Closing question: for a power‑constrained embedded L1, would you choose random or pseudo‑LRU, and what would guide your decision?

Policy overview
LRU: best for temporal locality, higher tracking cost
Random: lowest hardware cost, sometimes close in quality

Write considerations

Write-back requires dirty bits and write-back on eviction which increases bandwidth needs and energy; include these when evaluating replacement costs.

Common implementation mistakes

  • Assuming LRU is always worth its cost; measuring on traces is essential.

Pro tip

screens.title: Choosing Associativity for L1 and L2
screens.narratorSegment: When choosing associativity, think about the cache's role in the memory hierarchy and its latency budget. L1 caches serve the processor’s critical path and must be fast; this constrains L1 associativity to small values, typically 2–8 ways, because each additional way adds comparators and increases the access critical path. L2 caches have more relaxed latency requirements and can use higher associativity (8–16 ways) to reduce conflict misses for larger working sets. Another consideration is area and power: for area-limited designs, extra associativity can be costly in both silicon and power budget. Use the hands‑on design exercise to quantify tag overhead and comparator counts, then simulate access traces to measure hit‑rate improvements. A common misconception is that maximal associativity always benefits overall performance; increasing associativity can increase cycle time or access latency enough that net performance degrades. As a practical rule, aim for the smallest associativity that reaches near‑optimal hit rate on representative traces: often 4‑way is a sweet spot for L1 and 8‑way for L2. Finally, always validate with workload traces because the best choice depends on access patterns and system constraints.

screens.title: What to Remember

Also remember replacement policies: LRU improves hit rate at hardware cost; random is cheap and often adequate. Finally, validate all designs with real access traces because workload behavior determines whether extra associativity actually improves performance. If you remember these formulas and the practical tradeoffs, you can design and justify cache organizations for real systems.

fullNarratorScript:
Today we study three cache mapping strategies that determine where memory blocks live inside a cache. You will learn the defining property of each mapping, the step-by-step access procedure they use, and why associativity changes hit rate, access time, area, and power. We’ll ground the ideas with a 32 KB example so you can see actual numbers for lines, sets, and tag overhead. Understanding these mappings matters because the cache is the first hardware your processor relies on for speed: a wrong design increases misses, slows execution, and burns more power. For example, a direct‑mapped L1 is simple and very fast, but two hot blocks can repeatedly evict each other and cause conflict misses. A set‑associative design reduces those conflicts by giving blocks multiple candidate lines, and a fully‑associative cache eliminates conflict misses entirely at the cost of parallel tag comparisons and larger area. By the end you’ll be able to calculate index and tag bits, compare access-time tradeoffs, and make evidence-based choices for L1 and L2 design. Ask yourself as we go: for a given working set, when is extra associativity worth the hardware cost?

In this chapter you will build measurable skills that let you design and evaluate caches. First, you will learn to design and analyze a direct‑mapped cache: extracting index and offset bits, storing tags and valid/dirty bits, and detecting hits precisely. That skill matters because correct indexing and tag width are foundational to cache correctness and accurate area/power estimates. Second, you will implement set‑associative caches and understand replacement policies like least‑recently‑used and random replacement; you will see how the replacement policy affects effective hit rate and implementation complexity. Third, you will develop intuition for how associativity changes hit rate, access time, and power — including why returns diminish as associativity grows. Finally, you will calculate area and tag overhead for real cache designs, using formulas that combine data bits and tag bits. Each objective pairs a definition with a concrete calculation or small example so you can reason quantitatively. By the end you will be able to justify a cache organization for an L1 or L2 based on measured tradeoffs and simple area math.

We will assess your understanding with calculation tasks and a small design exercise. First, you should be able to compute index and offset bits from S, L, and A and derive tag bits for a given address width. For example, the assessment asks for index bits when a 32 KB cache uses 32‑byte lines and 4‑way associativity. You will also calculate the total tag storage in bits and the tag overhead percentage. Second, you will explain replacement policies: describe how LRU reduces conflict misses compared with random replacement, and when random is acceptable because of lower hardware cost. Third, you must interpret qualitative tradeoffs: given cache size and target latency, choose L1 associativity and justify your pick in 2–3 sentences. Finally, a hands‑on exercise asks you to compare three designs for a 32 KB cache (direct, 4‑way, 8‑way) and estimate expected hit rates qualitatively. These assessments emphasize reasoning: show calculations, state assumptions, and explain how associativity affects conflict and capacity misses. This prepares you to make practical cache design recommendations.

A direct‑mapped cache places each memory block into exactly one cache line determined by the block address modulo the number of cache lines. Practically, that means the address is partitioned into offset bits, index bits, and tag bits. The offset selects a byte within a line, the index selects a specific cache line, and the tag distinguishes different blocks that map to the same line. The access procedure is deterministic: extract the index, read the stored tag and valid bit for that line, compare tags, and if they match and valid is set, it's a hit; otherwise fetch from the next level. A concrete example helps: with a 32 KB cache and 64‑byte lines we have 512 lines; offset is 6 bits, index is 9 bits, and the remaining address bits form the tag. A common misconception is that direct mapping is always too poor for performance — in fact, for many streaming or tightly localized workloads it performs well due to its low latency and minimal hardware. The core tradeoff to watch for is conflict misses: two frequently used blocks that share the same index will repeatedly evict each other. A key takeaway is that direct mapping is the fastest and smallest design but you must consider access patterns to avoid pathological conflicts. How might your program’s stride create repeated conflicts?

A set‑associative cache generalizes direct mapping by grouping lines into sets and allowing a block to occupy any line within its set. The set index is computed as block address modulo the number of sets and the set contains N ways. Access proceeds by extracting the set index, then reading and comparing N tags and valid bits in parallel. If one matches and is valid, the access is a hit and the offset selects bytes within that way. If none match, a replacement is required: the cache chooses a victim line within the set according to the replacement policy — common policies are least‑recently‑used (LRU) and random replacement. A concrete example: a 4‑way, 32 KB cache with 64‑byte lines has 128 sets; each set stores four tags and four valid bits, and four comparators are used concurrently. A common misconception is that associativity alone removes all misses; it only eliminates conflict misses but not capacity or compulsory misses. The practical implication is that set associativity reduces conflicts with modest hardware cost when N is small, but returns diminish as N grows. Consider: if two hot blocks map to the same set, a 2‑way design may fix it, but increasing to 16‑way may add complexity without meaningful hit-rate gain. What replacement policy would you choose for a small embedded L1 cache and why?

A fully‑associative cache allows any memory block to occupy any cache line. There is no index; the cache compares the address tag against all stored tags simultaneously. This eliminates conflict misses because a block never has a fixed destination, but achieving this behavior requires comparators and search logic across the entire cache, which increases area and power. Fully associativity is therefore rare for large data caches but valuable for small structures where conflict should be avoided — for example, TLBs or small victim caches. A concrete example: a small 64‑line fully‑associative structure will compare one tag against 64 stored tags in parallel; hardware designers often use CAM‑style techniques or optimized comparators. A common misconception is that fully‑associative caches always give the best performance; they do minimize conflicts but their slower access time and power can make overall system performance worse if the comparator delay increases critical path latency. The main design question is cost versus conflict reduction. Reflect: for which small hardware structure could you afford full associativity and why? Fully‑Associative Cache Behavior means fully-associative caches remove conflict misses but cost significant comparators, area, and power; used where small size or special semantics justify it.. In practical terms, any line can hold any block; tags compared against all lines. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparing mapping types requires balancing four core metrics: hit rate, access time, area, and power. Direct‑mapped caches have the smallest area and lowest power because they need one comparator per access and minimal multiplexing, so access time is fastest. However, they suffer more conflict misses, giving the lowest hit rate in adversarial mapping scenarios. Set‑associative caches improve hit rate by offering multiple candidate lines per set; they need N comparators and multiplexers which increase area, power, and nominal access time in proportion to N. Fully‑associative caches give the highest hit rate because they eliminate conflict misses, but they are the most expensive in area and power and typically have the longest access latency because of the large number of parallel comparators. A useful rule of thumb drawn from practical systems: 2‑ to 8‑way associativity is common in L1 caches where low latency is critical; L2 caches may use higher associativity since their latency budget is larger. One misconception is that associativity always yields consistent benefit — in practice returns diminish as you increase associativity because remaining misses become capacity or compulsory misses. As a design question, ask whether the hit-rate gain from increasing associativity justifies the extra comparator and multiplexer cost for your target workload.

Computing offset, index, and tag bits is a fundamental step when designing caches. Start with line size L: offset bits equal log2(L) because the offset selects the byte within a line. Number of lines equals S divided by L. For associativity A, the number of sets equals S divided by (L × A), so index bits equal log2(number of sets). The remaining bits of the address width become the tag. Concretely, for a 32 KB cache with 64‑byte lines and 4‑way associativity: offset = log2(64) = 6, sets = 32768 / (64 × 4) = 128, index = log2(128) = 7, so tag = 32 - 6 - 7 = 19. A common error is forgetting to divide by associativity when computing sets — this produces an incorrect index width and wrong mapping. Below is a small code-like checklist you can use when doing the math yourself. Practice this computation on the three designs in the hands‑on exercise to see how index bits change between direct, 4‑way and 8‑way. Remember to include valid and dirty bits when calculating tag storage overhead.

Calculating cache area starts with the data array and the tag array. For a cache of size S, the data array stores S × 8 bits. The tag array stores a tag per line: tag bits plus one valid bit and one dirty bit for write‑back caches. The number of lines equals S divided by L, so tag storage in bits equals (S / L) × (T + 1 + 1), where T is the tag size in bits. The total area is data area plus tag area plus modest overhead for decoders, comparators, and multiplexers. A concrete example given in the chapter: with 64‑byte lines and 32‑bit addresses, the tag is about 20 bits plus 2 status bits, so the tag overhead per line is 22 bits, which is 22 / 512 = 4.3% for 64‑byte lines. For 32‑byte lines the overhead doubles to 8.6% because the denominator halves. A common mistake is omitting the valid and dirty bits when computing tag area — these add directly to the tag storage and can be nontrivial for small line sizes. When designing, inspect how line size affects overhead: larger lines reduce tag overhead but can increase wasted data transfer on partial-line utilization. What line size would you pick for a workload with frequent small random accesses?
